content.text: Install if missing, OR update if not already at the newest available version

✗ COMMON MISTAKE Looping a yum task over a package list instead of passing the whole list to name: in one task. Looping runs one SEPARATE transaction per package (slower, three times the overhead); passing a list runs everything in ONE Yum transaction — same end result, meaningfully less efficient the loop way.

package_facts gathers installed-package details into ansible_facts.packages, register-able and inspectable with debug — useful for a pre-flight check on what's already on a host before deciding what else to install.

yum only works where Yum/DNF is the package manager. Other operating systems need their own module — dnf (Fedora), apt (Debian/Ubuntu), win_package (Windows) — or, for a single task that should work anywhere, the generic package module, which auto-detects the right backend:

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT package is convenient but NOT a complete substitute for the specific module — it doesn't expose every specialized option yum/dnf/apt do, AND it doesn't solve the different-package-names problem (httpd on RHEL is apache2 on Ubuntu). A conditional selecting the right module AND the right package name per OS is still often necessary.
Registering systems with Red Hat Subscription Management
- name: Register and subscribe the system
One module call replaces both subscription-manager register and subscription-manager attach --pool= — state: present does both; state: absent unregisters.
description: Example Inc. Internal YUM repo

file: names the .repo file created under /etc/yum.repos.d/ (the extension is added automatically). With gpgcheck: yes, the required GPG public key must ALSO be installed separately with the rpm_key module — enabling the check without importing the key just makes every install from that repo fail signature verification.
- name: Add new user to the development machine and assign the appropriate groups

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT append: yes is the single most important detail in this whole section. Without it, groups: OVERWRITES the user's supplementary group membership entirely — any existing group not in the list gets silently removed. With append: yes, the listed groups are ADDED to whatever the user already belongs to. Forgetting append: yes is a classic way to accidentally strip a user's existing access.
- name: Create a SSH key for user1
generate_ssh_key never overwrites an existing key — safe to leave in a playbook that runs repeatedly.
groups: supplementary group LIST; group: the PRIMARY group (singular, one value)
yes/no — whether to create a home directory
yes marks this a system account — cannot be changed on an EXISTING user afterward
- name: Verify that auditors group exists
gid sets a specific GID; system: yes marks it a system group; local forces local (non-centralized) group commands on platforms that distinguish the two.
known_hosts and authorized_key — managing SSH trust at scale
- name: copy host keys to remote servers

Both use the lookup() plugin to read a key's content directly from a file on the CONTROL NODE at task-run time — a key can also be sourced straight from a URL (e.g. a GitHub public-keys URL) instead of a local file.

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS This pair is what makes onboarding/offboarding a team across dozens of servers a single playbook run instead of a manual, error-prone, per-server chore: authorized_key grants a new hire's key everywhere at once; removing it (state: absent) revokes it everywhere at once.

sections.title: 3. Managing the Boot Process and Scheduled Processes

content.text: How far in the future (must be used together — minutes/hours/days/weeks)
Run an existing script instead of an inline command
yes = don't schedule a duplicate if an equivalent job is already pending

This writes directly into the named user's crontab, in correct crontab syntax, automatically — no manual cron.d file editing required. special_time (reboot/yearly/monthly/weekly/daily/hourly) is a convenient shorthand for the common recurring schedules instead of spelling out minute/hour/day fields.
Basic: start/stop/restart/enable — works across older init systems too
Everything service does, PLUS daemon-reload and other systemd-specific behavior

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS Recognize the direct RH134 parallel: daemon-reload: yes here is exactly systemctl daemon-reload from RH134 Part 2 — same requirement, same reason (pick up a changed unit file), just expressed as a module parameter instead of a typed command.
The reboot module — safer than a raw reboot command

reboot shuts the managed host down, WAITS until it's back up and reachable again, then lets the play continue — a raw shell: reboot task would disconnect Ansible immediately and likely fail the play, since the connection drops before Ansible can confirm anything.
shell vs. command, and safely quoting variables
command is more restricted (no pipes, redirection, or shell features) but safer; shell allows full shell syntax but opens the door to injection if a variable's value isn't sanitized:
- name: Run a templated variable (always use quote filter to avoid injection)

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT Piping an untrusted or externally-sourced variable straight into a shell task without the | quote filter is a real injection risk — a filename or value containing shell metacharacters could execute something you never intended. Default to {{ var | quote }} any time a shell task's argument comes from a variable, not a literal.
This section is the RH134 Part 4 storage stack (partition → PV → VG → LV → filesystem → mount), expressed as Ansible modules instead of typed commands — the mental model doesn't change at all.
LVM: the lvg and lvol modules
Adding a physical volume to an existing VG is simply listing MORE devices in pvs: — lvg resizes the VG to match:
- name: Create a logical volume of 2GB
lvol's resizefs: yes and shrink parameters map directly onto RH134's lvextend + xfs_growfs/resize2fs two-step from Part 4 — but as ONE module call instead of two separate commands.

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT mount's state: present configures the /etc/fstab entry but does NOT mount it immediately; state: mounted both writes the fstab entry AND mounts it right now. This is directly analogous to the /etc/fstab-then-mount two-step from RH134 Part 4 — know which state value you actually need.
Swap: no dedicated module, same manual steps
Ansible has no swap-specific module — the RH134 manual sequence (create LV, mkswap, swapon) is simply expressed via lvg/lvol plus command tasks for the parts with no module:

ansible_swaptotal_mb (a standard fact) makes this idempotent-ish in intent — the mkswap task only runs when swap is genuinely low, though command itself still isn't natively idempotent (Part 3's caveat about command/shell modules applies directly here).

Two approaches, same as storage had two approaches (manual modules vs. Stratis): the network RHEL System Role (declarative, recommended), or individual modules (nmcli, hostname, firewalld) for finer-grained control.

network_provider selects the backend — nm (NetworkManager, the RHEL 8 default) or initscripts (RHEL 6-style, requires the network service). network_connections is a list of connection dictionaries, each with state (up/down — runtime) and persistent_state (present/absent — survives reboot) as separate, independently-controllable settings.
hostname sets ONLY the system hostname — it deliberately does NOT touch /etc/hosts, so a stale /etc/hosts entry can still cause DNS-adjacent confusion after a rename unless handled separately.

🎯 RHCE-RELEVANT The firewalld module has the exact same permanent-vs-immediate trap as firewall-cmd from RH134 Part 6: permanent: yes alone saves the change for future boots but does NOT necessarily apply it to the CURRENTLY running firewall. Add immediate: yes to also apply it right now, in the same task — mirroring firewall-cmd --permanent needing --reload.

gather_subset narrows fact-gathering to just one category (faster than gathering everything); filter then narrows further to one specific fact name using shell-style wildcards. ansible_NICNAME (e.g. ansible_ens4) gives full per-interface detail — IPv4/IPv6 addresses, MAC, MTU, active state — for a specific named interface.

labs.title: Lab: Provision a Complete Web Server — End to End

content.text: Combine all five domains from this Part into one playbook: software, a service account, boot/scheduling, storage, and network/firewall — a realistic, complete server-provisioning play.

Provision a new web server from a bare RHEL 8 host: install and enable httpd, create a dedicated service account with correct group membership, mount a dedicated LVM-backed volume for web content, schedule a nightly log rotation reminder, and open the firewall correctly — permanently AND immediately.
One RHEL 8 managed host with an unused virtual disk /dev/vdb, reachable via Ansible
1. Install httpd, mod_ssl, httpd-tools in one efficient yum task (list form, not a loop)
2. Create a service account webadmin, added to the apache group with append: yes (so any existing groups aren't wiped)
3. Build a full storage stack for /var/www/content: partition /dev/vdb, PV/VG (vg_web), LV (lv_web, 1g), XFS filesystem, mounted persistently (state: mounted, not just present)
4. Add a cron job running a log-check script nightly at 02:00 as webadmin
5. Open the http service in firewalld, both permanent AND immediate
6. Start and enable httpd with the systemd module

Remember the mount module's two relevant state values from Section 8.4 — present only configures fstab, mounted configures fstab AND mounts right now. You want the content directory usable immediately, not just after a future reboot.

Before checking the solution: did you remember immediate: yes on the firewalld task? Without it, the http rule is correctly saved for next boot but the CURRENTLY running firewall keeps blocking it — exactly the RH134 --permanent/--reload trap, just under a different module.
- name: Create web content volume group
- name: Create web content logical volume
The yum task installs all three packages in one transaction — deliberately not a loop, per Section 8.1's efficiency guidance.
append: yes on the user task means webadmin's group membership only ever grows via this playbook — it never wipes an unrelated group added by someone else.
state: mounted (not present) on the mount task ensures /var/www/content is usable the moment this playbook finishes, not only after a future reboot.
immediate: yes alongside permanent: yes on the firewalld task means the currently-running firewall opens the port THIS run, not just on next boot.

curl http://<host> should succeed immediately after the playbook finishes (proving httpd is running AND the firewall is genuinely open right now, not just configured for later). df -h /var/www/content should show the new LVM volume mounted. Running the whole playbook a second time should report changed=0 across every task.

This lab is, functionally, a complete real-world server-provisioning playbook — the same shape (packages, accounts, storage, scheduling, firewall, service) that a genuine production onboarding playbook would have, just scaled down. Everything from RH124 through this Part has been building toward exactly this kind of end-to-end automation.
Q1. Why is passing a list to yum's name: parameter more efficient than looping the yum task over a list?
Answer: A list installs everything in ONE Yum transaction; looping runs one SEPARATE transaction per package, with more overhead.
Q2. What does the generic package module trade away for its cross-distribution convenience?

Answer: It doesn't expose every specialized option the OS-specific modules (yum/dnf/apt) do, and it doesn't solve differing package names across distributions — a conditional may still be needed for that.
Q3. What does forgetting append: yes on a user task's groups: parameter actually do?
Answer: It OVERWRITES the user's supplementary group membership — any existing group not in the list gets silently removed, instead of the listed groups being added to what's already there.
Q4. What's the practical difference between the service and systemd Ansible modules?
Answer: service offers the basic start/stop/restart/enable set and works across older init systems; systemd offers everything service does plus systemd-specific behavior like daemon-reload.
Q5. Why is the reboot module safer than a shell: reboot task?
Answer: reboot shuts the host down and WAITS until it's back up and reachable before continuing the play; a raw shell reboot disconnects Ansible immediately and would likely fail the task/play.
Q6. What's the security risk of putting an unsanitized variable directly into a shell task, and how is it mitigated?
Answer: Shell metacharacters in the variable's value could cause unintended command execution (injection); mitigate with the quote filter, e.g. {{ var | quote }}.
Q7. What's the difference between mount's state: present and state: mounted?
Answer: present only configures the /etc/fstab entry; mounted configures fstab AND mounts the device immediately.
Q8. Does Ansible have a dedicated module for configuring swap space?
Answer: No — swap is configured using the same lvg/lvol modules as any other LVM storage, plus command tasks for mkswap/swapon, which have no dedicated module.
Q9. In the network system role, what's the difference between a connection's state and persistent_state?
Answer: state (up/down) is the connection's RUNTIME status right now; persistent_state (present/absent) controls whether the connection profile survives a reboot.
Q10. What must be added to a firewalld module task alongside permanent: yes to make the change take effect on the CURRENTLY running firewall, not just after the next reboot?
Answer: immediate: yes — the same permanent-vs-apply-now trap as firewall-cmd --permanent needing --reload in RH134.
RH294 — RED HAT SYSTEM ADMINISTRATION III: LINUX AUTOMATION

This closes out the RH294 guide — and with it, the full RH124 → RH134 → RH294 curriculum. Like RH134 Part 8, this isn't new material: a condensed cross-chapter review, one large capstone playbook that forces every RH294 chapter to work together, an automation skill checklist, and a final mixed quiz.

💡 WHY THIS MATTERS A real Ansible project never exercises just one chapter's worth of knowledge — a single playbook touches inventory, variables, task control, templates, roles, and troubleshooting all at once. This Part is built the same way, on purpose.
